title: Balance a payload deck with two ballast blocks
instruction: Place both grey ballast blocks flat on the white deck so that the combined centre of mass of the gold instrument and the two blocks lies over the deck's centre mark, within 5 mm horizontally. The instrument is 300 g, the large block 120 g and the small block 60 g.
context: Spacecraft and payloads are statically balanced before spin tests and launch: the centre of mass is measured on a mass-properties table and balance masses are fixed at computed places until it sits on the spin axis. This tabletop analogue keeps the computation. A gold instrument is glued 60 mm off the centre of a white deck, and two grey ballast blocks of one density, a 60 g cube and a 120 g bar, must go onto the deck so the combined centre of mass lands on the centre mark. Together the blocks are lighter than the instrument, so the obvious placements fail: both at the mark leave it 37.5 mm off, and both opposite the instrument at its own distance leave it 15 mm off. The masses are stated; the offset is read from the scene and the moments weighed in both axes. Many placements succeed. The score is a property of where both blocks go together, so it tests physical reasoning about moments. No microgravity is claimed.
setup: Table coordinates in metres: x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y left from the midline, z up; the table top is the zero of every height below, and the arm bases are at y = +0.305 (left) and y = -0.305 (right). Everything is in the left arm's reach; the right arm is idle at its ready pose. Fixed parts, matte: the deck, a white (sRGB 0.92, 0.92, 0.90) square plate 260 x 260 x 12 mm with its edges along x and y, centred at (0.250, 0.260), spanning x 0.120 to 0.380 and y 0.130 to 0.390, its top 12 mm above the table; the centre mark, a black (sRGB 0.05, 0.05, 0.05) cross of two bars 40 x 10 mm, one along x and one along y, crossing at the deck centre (0.250, 0.260) and standing 0.5 mm proud of the deck; the instrument, a gold (sRGB 0.85, 0.65, 0.15) box 70 x 50 x 45 mm (x, y, z) glued to the deck with its edges along x and y, centred at (0.298, 0.296), which is 48 mm forward of the mark and 36 mm to its left (60 mm away), spanning x 0.263 to 0.333 and y 0.271 to 0.321, its top 57 mm above the table; its stated mass is 300 g, with its centre of mass over the centre of its footprint. Loose parts, grey (sRGB 0.40, 0.42, 0.45), matte, both of one density (about 2.2 g/cm3), so mass follows volume: the large block, a bar 60 x 30 x 30 mm, 120 g, standing on a 60 x 30 face with its long axis along x, centred at (0.180, 0.470); the small block, a 30 mm cube, 60 g, with its faces along x and y, centred at (0.280, 0.470). Both start on the table 80 mm left of the deck's left edge (centre to edge) and 55 mm apart edge to edge. Nominal end state, the scripted demo's: the bar flat along x centred at (0.170, 0.220), 80 mm behind and 40 mm right of the mark, and the cube centred at (0.170, 0.160), 80 mm behind and 100 mm right of the mark (it lands turned 15 degrees, which does not matter); then 300 g x (48, 36) mm + 120 g x (-80, -40) mm + 60 g x (-80, -100) mm = (0, 0), so the combined centre of mass sits on the mark. For reference, a balance needs the blocks' combined moment to be 18,000 g mm directed away from the instrument, for example both blocks 100 mm from the mark on the side opposite it. To build it: cut the deck from 12 mm plywood or acrylic, paint it white and tape it to the table; mark the cross at its centre with 10 mm black tape; make the instrument from a 70 x 50 x 45 mm wooden or printed box wrapped in gold foil and glue it to the deck at the stated place (its real mass does not matter, the score uses the stated 300 g); machine both blocks from solid PTFE (about 2.2 g/cm3, so 59 g and 119 g) and cover them in grey matte vinyl, or print both as closed hollow shells from the same filament and fill each evenly with a weighed mix of steel shot and epoxy to 60 g and 120 g, so the centre of mass stays at the block centre; tape the two start marks.
scoring: Judged on the end state after the arm has released and withdrawn; in simulation on the final step (SCORE_OVER end). A block counts as on the deck when it rests flat on the deck plate: one face down with a tilt under 5 degrees (any face and any yaw, so the bar may lie or stand on end), its lowest point within 4 mm of the deck top, its centre over the deck (inside the 260 x 260 mm outline; an overhanging edge is fine), and at rest (under 10 mm/s and 0.5 rad/s). A block on the table, on the instrument, on the other block, tilted against something, moving or still held counts as missing. With a tape, measure each counted block's centre from the mark along x (xL, xS) and along y (yL, yS) in mm, and compute the combined centre of mass of the instrument and the counted blocks: X = (300 x 48 + 120 x xL + 60 x xS) / M and Y = (300 x 36 + 120 x yL + 60 x yS) / M, where M is 300 g plus the masses of the counted blocks and a missing block's term is left out; the error is the square root of X squared plus Y squared. Score: both blocks counted and the error at most 5 mm, 1.0, the success condition, which ends the trial once it has held for 1 s; at most 10 mm, 0.5; at most 12.5 mm, 0.25; more than 12.5 mm, 0. With only one block counted, the same ladder capped at 0.25; with none, 0, so the start state scores 0. Every outcome falls in exactly one tier. A value exactly on a limit passes, with a 0.1 mm margin. A 5 mm error in the combined centre of mass equals 20 mm of error in the bar's place alone or 40 mm in the cube's, so a tape measure is ample. Reference outcomes: the demo's nominal placement, 0 mm, 1.0; the two blocks' joint centre of mass 100 mm from the mark directly opposite the instrument, 0 mm, 1.0, and 120 mm from it, 7.5 mm, 0.5; that joint centre 60 mm opposite, mirroring the instrument, 15 mm, 0; both blocks at the mark, 37.5 mm, 0; the bar opposite the instrument at 60 mm and the cube on the mark, 22.5 mm, 0; the bar alone at the demo's spot, 18.3 mm, 0; the bar alone 150 mm directly opposite the instrument, where it balances it by itself, 0 mm, capped at 0.25; the cube alone earns nothing, since even centred on the deck's corner opposite the instrument it leaves 20.1 mm. Pushing cannot place a block, because the deck stands 12 mm proud of the table and a block tipped onto its edge is not flat. In simulation every horizontal test and the bottom height use the block centres and quaternions, not the axis-aligned bounds, and the deck, the mark and the instrument are fixed; the scorer cannot see the gripper, so a block held perfectly still in a passing pose reads as placed; on the real rig the photo after the arm withdraws decides, and a trial in which the deck or the instrument moves scores 0.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Stand the bar back on its mark with its long axis along x and the cube on its mark with its faces along x and y; the deck, the mark and the instrument do not move.
fidelity: Approximate: rigid primitives sharing one matte material (friction 1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic); the deck, mark and instrument are static colliders. The masses are stated, not sensed: the score computes the centre of mass from the stated 300, 120 and 60 g and the block positions, with the deck's own mass centred and left out. A real balance job measures the imbalance on a mass-properties table; here it follows from the stated masses and the visible offset.
